text.en: Asha's lunch box had rice, dal, vegetables and a fruit. "A balanced meal," said her mother.

Food provides material for growth, repair, energy and other body functions. Different foods supply different combinations of nutrients. The classes of nutrients are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water. Vitamin D is called the sunshine vitamin because exposure to sunlight can help the skin make it. Some foods also supply vitamin D.
Food hygiene includes clean handling and storage practices that help reduce the chance of contamination. Food preservation slows spoilage and can make some foods last longer. Different methods use changes in temperature, moisture or other conditions.
Food adulteration includes adding an unauthorised substance, substituting an ingredient or removing something valuable from a food in a way that compromises its quality. Food quality control, with standards and tests, keeps food safe.

The classes of nutrients are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water.

Food quality control, with standards and tests, keeps food safe.
Carbohydrates are an important source of energy. Rice and other grains often contain starch, which is a carbohydrate made of linked sugar units.
Proteins are used in growth, repair and many body processes. Beans, lentils, dairy foods, eggs and other foods can provide proteins.
Fats can provide energy and are used in cells. Some vitamins are absorbed along with fat. The source and the overall mixture of foods both matter.

board.text: Fats provide energy and aid absorption of some vitamins

text.en: Vitamins are needed in relatively small amounts. They serve different functions. For example, vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium.
Minerals include calcium and iron. Calcium contributes to bones, and iron is part of the haemoglobin that carries oxygen in red blood cells.

board.text: Calcium and iron have different jobs

text.en: Water helps move dissolved substances and regulate body temperature. Fibre is found in many plant foods and helps material move through the digestive tract.

board.text: Water and fibre support body functions

text.en: No single everyday food supplies all nutrients in the same amounts. Comparing a grain, a pulse and a vegetable shows why variety matters.
A balanced diet is a pattern that provides enough energy and nutrients for the person. Needs can vary during growth and with activity. A single fictional plate does not capture everyone’s needs.

board.text: Needs can vary with growth and activity

text.en: Malnutrition can result from too little energy, too much energy, an imbalance or shortages of particular nutrients. It is a broad word about nutrition.

board.text: Malnutrition includes several kinds of imbalance

text.en: The textbook describes protein-energy malnutrition as inadequate intake or availability of protein and energy. Signs can have several causes, so a textbook picture cannot diagnose an individual.
A nutrition label states quantities for a specified amount of food. Check whether that reference is one serving or a fixed mass before comparing two products.
If a fictional food lists four grams of protein per serving, two of those servings supply eight grams. The number of servings changes the total, while the value per serving stays the same.
Food can be contaminated if material passes from an unclean surface or utensil to food. Food hygiene looks at the path by which contamination can happen.
Cooling slows many processes that spoil food. Drying reduces available water. Both can make a difference without making a food last forever.

board.text: Cooling slows change · drying removes water

text.en: Heating can reduce many microorganisms when used in a controlled process. Pasteurisation is a commercial example that uses a managed combination of heating and time.
Preservation can also use packaging or permitted substances that help a product keep its quality. The choice depends on the food and what kind of change needs to be limited.

board.text: Match preservation to the kind of spoilage

text.en: Food irradiation is a regulated industrial process that uses radiation to reduce certain pests or microorganisms in some products. It is distinct from adding a substance to the food.
Spoilage describes unwanted changes that can affect smell, texture or appearance. Some food-safety hazards cause no visible change, so appearance alone cannot settle whether a product is safe.
Adulteration can include substituting a cheaper ingredient and failing to declare the substitution. The problem is the change to what the food is expected to contain.

board.text: An undeclared substitution changes the product

text.en: Quality control includes checking that batches meet standards for identity, consistency and safety. A single check is only one part of the evidence.

board.text: Quality control compares a product with standards

text.en: A packaged food label can show its ingredients, a batch number and the date information. Those details answer different questions about composition, traceability and storage.
Compare food hygiene with preservation. Hygiene aims to reduce contamination during handling. Preservation aims to slow or reduce unwanted changes during storage.

board.text: Handling and storage address different questions

text.en: When reading a claim about food, identify which nutrient, process or quality measure it describes. Ask what is measured and what evidence the claim offers.

board.text: Identify the claim and its evidence

problem.en: A fictional packet lists 4 g protein per 30 g serving. How much protein is listed for two servings?

text.en: Read the amount for one serving.

why.en: The label reports four grams of protein for thirty grams of food.

text.en: Multiply the amount per serving by two.

why.en: Two servings list eight grams of protein.

prompt.en: A friend says Adulterated food is always safe. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: Adulteration mixes in cheap or harmful substances.

points.en: A balanced diet has all nutrients.
Sunlight can help skin make vitamin D. Some foods also supply it.
